source_title: 7 Most Unplayable RPG Masterpieces Of All Time, Ranked - GameRant
source_excerpt:
RPGs have existed for many decades now, and in that time, we have been graced with a huge number of masterpieces of all shapes and sizes. However, as time goes by, not all of them have aged well , and some of the best games the genre has ever seen have unfortunately become borderline unplayable by modern standards.
That isn't to take away from the greatness these games once represented, and there is still an argument that their stories and worlds hold up today, even if their gameplay doesn't. But when you actually start exploring and engaging on a deeper level, it becomes clear that maybe some games are better left in the past.
Interactive world was way ahead of the curve.
Clunky combat and other awkward systems.
Ultima 7: The Black Gate remains one of the most ambitious RPGs ever created, featuring a living world where NPCs follow daily routines and nearly every object can be manipulated. You have so much freedom to explore and engage with the world however you choose, and that freedom helped establish a lot of RPG principles that modern games still follow.
Sign in to claim your place on the leaderboard!
Unfortunately, its age creates substantial barriers, even for die-hard RPG fans. The interface is cumbersome, inventory management is awkward, and the real-time combat can feel clunky. If, like me, you aren't too familiar with older RPG conventions, the experience will end up feeling pretty poor despite the greatness hidden within.
6 Might And Magic 6: The Mandate Of Heaven
Enormous world with extraordinary freedom.
Dated design and unforgiving encounters.
Might and Magic 6: The Mandate of Heaven is a textbook CRPG, presenting you with a tremendous world filled with sprawling dungeons and dangerous enemies, and you have just the party to deal with them. The first-person perspective makes exploration feel much more immersive, while the sheer scale of the adventure allows you to really get lost in the world as you level up and grow stronger over time.
All of that comes with the massive caveats of chaotic combat and poorly designed interfaces that lack the comfort found in games today. If you are willing to learn its systems, you will find a deeply rewarding RPG, but I can also appreciate how the rough edges may be an instant turnoff.
The Witcher translated the dark fantastical world of the Sapkowski books to the video game medium, and did so as faithfully as possible. Playing as Geralt in this form gives you an inside look at the early days of his story, and much like the later entries, the story is the big standout, with every NPC and questline offering enough flavor to keep you interested for dozens of hours.
However, in order to actually see those stories, you have to do a fair bit of fighting, and it is safe to say the combat is far from fluid. The timed sequences are sluggish and don't have the same impact as those in Wild Hunt or even Assassins of Kings , so if you really want more Witcher action, I'd suggest taking a look at the books instead of wading through the pains of the first game.
Slow opening and complicated systems overwhelm newcomers.
Wizardry 8 is a landmark in traditional party-based RPG design, offering extensive character customization and a more tactical style of turn-based combat that places a major emphasis on party composition. The class combinations encourage you to experiment and try new things, and outside of combat, you get to build relationships with each member, leading to some interesting narrative outcomes in almost every case.
The biggest barrier to accessing all those great elements is the sheer complexity of the game. Fights can turn into lengthy encounters that feel punishing on defeat, and the management of an entire party proves very intimidating, making it yet another classic that is arguably too cumbersome and ambitious for modern players to handle.
Grim story provides an unusual hook.
Repetitive battles make the original hard to recommend.
Drakengard already stands out with its extremely bleak setting, but the story is where it really excels. It explores themes of obsession and madness and has you engaging in some seriously unsettling sequences that almost always end in the most unexpected way possible.
That's all great, but the combat that links those moments together starts to get very repetitive, especially when the fights become wars of attrition rather than tests of skill. It's a reflection of the PS2 era, and a relic best left on the shelf gathering dust. If you want a darker experience from an RPG, there are far better modern examples out there.
Immersive world that grows with you.
Punishing fights that feel borderline unfair.
Gothic was always known for its brutal difficulty, and that is both its biggest strength and weakness. You start out incredibly weak and need to pick your fights carefully, slowly gathering the strength to take on tougher foes and venture into more dangerous territory.
That progression looks pretty simple and expected from an RPG, yet because of how stiff the controls are, you end up wrestling more with your inputs than the actual enemies. In some cases, playing the original can be better than the remake, but I would argue that you're not missing much by playing the Gothic Remake instead, and will have a whole lot more fun with the contemporary version.
Gigantic world that requires a lot of traveling.
Old-school design proves too much for modern players.
The Elder Scrolls 2: Daggerfall has a lot of prestige on its shoulders, and one of the main reasons it still gets talked about is its map size. The landscape is vast, and you can wander off in one direction and encounter dozens of quests and dungeons, each filled to the brim with loot and treasures beyond your wildest dreams.
As ambitious and far-reaching as the map may be, because of its procedural nature, many locations start to get repetitive, which is made worse by the almost alien control scheme that immediately gates many modern players. I can understand being an Elder Scrolls fan and wanting to revisit the classics, yet as exciting as it sounds, Daggerfall is a borderline chore to get through, even if you have the patience to deal with it.
